brief:
No Arab official sat closer to the region's negotiating tables for longer than Sheikh Hamad bin Jassim bin Jaber Al Thani, Qatar's foreign minister from 1992 to 2013 and its prime minister from 2007 to 2013. When he says he knows something about the death of Yasser Arafat, Palestinians listen — and argue.

His most explosive testimony came in the "Black Box" interview series with the Kuwaiti journalist Ammar Taqi, broadcast on the Al-Qabas platform in February 2022. Arafat, he said, "was definitely killed by someone close to him."

He has never walked that sentence back. Through a string of interviews and statements since — the latest an hour-long appearance on Al Jazeera's The Interview in May 2026 and a widely shared post this month — the former premier has kept returning to Palestine, and the Arafat file has followed him.

## The meeting in his Doha office

The heart of his account is a meeting he says took place in his own office. "Several months before his illness, a meeting was held in my office in Doha attended by Palestinian figures and representatives of the Israeli side," he told the program, "and we discussed all the mechanisms by which Arafat could get out of the crisis safely, to outside Palestine."

Arafat was then in his third year confined to the wreckage of the Muqataa compound in Ramallah, under an Israeli siege that began in 2002, while Israeli ministers debated expelling him outright. Proposals for a negotiated departure circulated through several capitals in those years; Hamad bin Jassim's account places one strand of them in Doha, with both sides in the room.

Then, he said, the channel simply closed. "A short time later, the parties I had met announced there was no need to continue discussing the issue."

> "The sudden change in Arafat's health indicates that something was being plotted against him — perhaps someone gave Arafat something in order to finish him off."
> Hamad bin Jassim, the Black Box interview, February 2022

Pressed on whether he was alleging murder, he refused the framing. "These are not claims," he said. "This is the truth." He named no individual, produced no document, and has offered none since.

## What the forensic record actually says

Arafat fell suddenly ill in October 2004, was flown to the Percy military hospital outside Paris, and died there on 11 November 2004 at 75. French doctors recorded a stroke brought on by a blood disorder and identified no poison at the time.

The file reopened in 2012, when an Al Jazeera investigation prompted Switzerland's Institute of Radiation Physics in Lausanne to test his personal effects and report traces of polonium-210. His widow, Suha Arafat, won a French murder inquiry and an exhumation of his body in Ramallah that November.

The science then split three ways. The Lausanne team's 2013 report found polonium levels in his ribs and pelvis up to eighteen times normal and concluded the results "moderately support" poisoning — the scientists put their confidence at around 83 percent. A Russian team found the evidence insufficient.

French court experts attributed the radioactivity to environmental radon in the tomb, and in 2015 French judges closed the case, ruling it had not been demonstrated that Arafat was murdered by polonium poisoning — a conclusion the Swiss scientists publicly called "debatable" and Suha Arafat's lawyers called biased.

The European Court of Human Rights later declined to reopen the probe.

The Palestinian Authority's own investigating committee, led by Tawfiq Tirawi, has for its part insisted Arafat was assassinated and placed the responsibility on Israel, which denies it. That is the unresolved record onto which Hamad bin Jassim dropped a different accusation entirely: not the occupier's hand, but a hand inside the house.

## Ramallah's silence, and the pushback

No official Palestinian body answered him. Neither the presidency, nor Fatah, nor the Tirawi committee issued a response to the Qatari's charge, a silence Arab outlets noted at the time.

The pushback came instead from commentators: the Palestinian outlet Amad ran a column dismissing the series as a "black box of lies," and Fatah loyalists asked why a man who sat on such knowledge for eighteen years produced it on a Kuwaiti talk show.

The former premier himself later complained that the broadcaster had cut segments from more than fifteen episodes of the series, saying he had been promised the interviews would air uncut — leaving open the question of what else the Black Box held.

## What else he says about Palestine

If the Arafat charge made him notorious in Ramallah, the rest of his Palestine record runs in a different direction.

In May 2024, as the war on Gaza entered its eighth month, he warned on X of a "plan to liquidate the Palestinian cause" and to bury the two-state solution, writing that only a united Palestinian front across Gaza and the West Bank could defeat it, the Middle East Monitor reported.

In December 2025 he returned with a prescription: comprehensive Palestinian elections open to every faction and community — "whether in Gaza, the West Bank or the diaspora" — to produce national reconciliation and "a Palestinian president capable of shouldering the responsibilities of the coming phase."

He urged the Arab League to back the vote and Palestinians to keep their ambitions "within the bounds of reality, so that the current deadlock does not continue, because the coming stage for the Palestinians will be delicate and existential."

His fullest recent accounting came on Al Jazeera's The Interview with Ali al-Dhafiri in May 2026. He condemned the killing of civilians on every side, then called Israel's response in Gaza a "moral and political disaster" that has killed more than 72,500 Palestinians and eroded Israel's narrative across Europe and the United States.

!video[Hamad bin Jassim's May 2026 interview on Al Jazeera's The Interview](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=U6CQEx2tobY)

In the same conversation he warned of a depopulation project, saying he had information that money was being offered to encourage Palestinians to leave Gaza — turning the strip, in his words, into "a real estate project."

He rejected any disarmament of Hamas without a guaranteed political horizon toward an independent Palestinian state, praised Saudi Arabia's refusal to normalize with Israel without a roadmap to statehood, and accused Benjamin Netanyahu of using the Iran war to market a "Greater Israel" and force a reshaped region.

The greatest danger to the Gulf, he added, is neither Iran nor Israel but Arab division, and he has since urged a collective Arab defense arrangement.

He was blunter still this month. "What is happening now in Gaza is crimes against humanity committed by Israel," he wrote on X on 5 August, in a post CNN Arabic reported, reminding readers how many committees had been formed to stop the war and how little they had stopped.

## A witness who keeps the file open

Hamad bin Jassim's Arafat testimony remains what it was in 2022: the recollection of a uniquely placed mediator, specific about the room and the timing, empty of names and evidence, and contradicted by no one because no one with authority has engaged it. The forensic record is frozen — polonium found, poisoning unproven, the French file closed, the Palestinian file officially open and officially aimed at Israel.

What he keeps demonstrating, from the elections call to the "real estate project" warning, is that the man who ran two decades of Qatar's diplomacy considers the Palestinian question unfinished business — including, insistently, the question of how its most famous leader died.
